paras: The Presidents Island workhouse beatings were assaults on prisoners at the county workhouse on Presidents Island, near Memphis, Tennessee, described by Black prisoners to a county court committee that visited on 28 March 1881. Prisoners said Deputy Sheriff Collins and two guards had struck them with an iron poker, a pistol and sticks and whipped them with a barrel stave. The Memphis papers headlined the report for the filth it found, and the committee later said it was satisfied that no cruel treatment was practiced.

The county quarterly court had appointed magistrates A. C. Welborn, C. E. Smith, P. M. Winters and James Brett to report on the workhouse on Presidents Island. Arriving at noon on 28 March, they judged the food adequate but found the bedding in the room for Black prisoners "wretchedly filthy", a privy inside the sleeping room, and prisoners who had not changed their clothes in memory. White prisoners were at work in a distant field during the visit, so nearly all the testimony on treatment came from Black prisoners.

John Jones, described as colored, was found sick in his bunk after two weeks on the island. He said that when he complained to Collins that he could not eat the food, the deputy jabbed him in the sides and struck him on the head with an iron poker and a pistol. Other prisoners told the committee they had seen it, but the committee found only a small scab on his head, which Jones attributed to the pistol.

Charlie Marshall, also described as colored, said Collins had beaten him with an iron poker and showed peeled knuckles. Archie Tindall said Collins whipped him because he was afraid to sit up with a sick man, and that he saw a Mr. Stinson strike Robert Butler and Henry Eppes with his fist and sticks. Eppes said a guard the Appeal called Lockery had whipped him with a barrel stave without cause. According to the Public Ledger, Joseph Williams, a former convict serving as a guard, said he saw Dockery, a former guard, whip Butler and strike Jim Rogers over the head with a navy six.

Anthony Sexton, a prisoner of about ten days, said he had seen no one whipped, though he did not stay in the colored ward. Collins and Stinson answered only on care of the sick, saying the guard tended them and that an employee named Foster, who had studied medicine, prescribed for them.

The committee reported to the county court on 4 April, offering no advice because its members drew different conclusions. The court continued the committee and added Chairman Holman, County Attorney Taylor, Judge Horrigan and Attorney-General Turner for a new investigation. Its next report, printed on 13 April, said the committee was satisfied that no cruel treatment of prisoners was practiced but that cleanliness was neglected.

On the committee's recommendation, the court then named the jail inspectors, county attorney and sheriff a standing committee to visit the workhouse. No charge against Collins, Stinson or Lockery appears in the coverage. In July the attorney-general declared void a county court order allowing corporal punishment of Presidents Island convicts.

Both Memphis dailies covered the report on 5 April. The Appeal printed it at length under the headline "FOUL AND FILTHY," with the prisoners' charges under subheads such as "JOHN JONES'S STATEMENT," and a local paragraph noted "other complaints as to whipping and ill-treatment." Its editorial page called the conditions "disgraceful in the extreme" to the county and urged churchwomen to visit the prisons, without mentioning the beatings.

The Public Ledger's shorter "THE ISLAND BELOW" gave more of the violence, adding Marshall's knuckles and Williams's account, while a one-line item treated the workhouse menu as "a current topic." A week later the Ledger printed the committee's finding of no cruel treatment without comment.

The prisoners' testimony, including corroboration of Jones, stands against the committee's own finding of a single small scab and its later conclusion that no cruel treatment was practiced. The committee itself called its evidence incomplete, and the papers name Butler's attacker differently: Stinson in Tindall's account, Dockery in Williams's.
